```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
options(width = 110)    # the code font is small, so let printed output run wider
# Paint the figure device the slide color, so plots with a fixed aspect ratio
# (coord_equal) don't sit in a white box
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(bg = "#F7F7F7"))

# 2024 CES Common Content (data/prepare_data.R builds the extract from the
# full release). Running example: family income, where about 8.5% of
# respondents pick the explicit "Prefer not to say" option. The outcome is
# inc60, family income of $60,000 or more (about the median among those who
# answer); R = 1 if the respondent answered.
# Covariates: age, gender, education, race, employment, marital status, party
# ID and political engagement (unsure: the number of "not sure" / "don't know"
# answers on four political items), observed for everyone in the extract.
# weight is the CES common weight, saved for next week
ces <- read_csv("data/ces24_income.csv") |>
  mutate(R = 1L - refused)

theme_md <- theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(colour = "#333333"),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F7F7F7", colour = NA))
```

```{r}
#| label: strip-setup
#| include: false

# Draws for the strip animation (strip-anim/strip.js), which runs across the
# intro, MAR and IPW slides. F is a 50/50 mixture of two normals, one per value
# of a binary covariate X: Y | X = 0 ~ N(3.5, 1.2^2), Y | X = 1 ~ N(6.5, 1.2^2),
# so mu = E[Y] = 5.
set.seed(812)
st_N <- 24; st_K <- 8; st_S <- 400
st_n <- 10                   # SRS: observe n of the N units
st_pi <- c(0.3, 0.8)         # Pr(R_i = 1 | X_i = 0), Pr(R_i = 1 | X_i = 1)
st_mean <- c(3.5, 6.5); st_sd <- 1.2
draw_F <- function() {
  x <- rbinom(st_N, 1, 0.5)
  list(x = x, y = pmin(pmax(rnorm(st_N, st_mean[x + 1], st_sd), 0.3), 9.7))
}

# Scene A: S i.i.d. samples of N units from F. The last one animated becomes
# the finite population, so it is redrawn until X splits 12/12, which keeps
# both groups visible when units go missing by X
st_A <- replicate(st_S, draw_F(), simplify = FALSE)
while (sum(st_A[[st_K]]$x) != st_N / 2) st_A[[st_K]] <- draw_F()
pop <- st_A[[st_K]]
mu_N <- mean(pop$y)

# Scene B: simple random sampling, n of the N units observed
st_B <- replicate(st_S, as.integer(seq_len(st_N) %in% sample(st_N, st_n)), simplify = FALSE)

# Scene C: R_i ~ Bernoulli(pi(X_i)), independently. A draw that leaves a group
# with no observed unit is redrawn (both estimators need one in each group).
# Complete-case mean, and the Hajek estimator with the known pi(X)
draw_R <- function() {
  repeat {
    r <- rbinom(st_N, 1, st_pi[pop$x + 1])
    if (all(tapply(r, pop$x, sum) > 0)) return(r)
  }
}
st_C <- replicate(st_S, draw_R(), simplify = FALSE)
hajek <- function(r) { w <- r / st_pi[pop$x + 1]; sum(w * pop$y) / sum(w) }

strip_data <- jsonlite::toJSON(list(
  N = st_N, n = st_n, K = st_K, ylim = c(0, 10), pi = st_pi,
  dens = list(w1 = 0.5, m0 = st_mean[1], m1 = st_mean[2], s = st_sd),
  mu = sum(0.5 * st_mean), muN = mu_N,
  ay = lapply(st_A[1:st_K], function(s) round(s$y, 3)), fx = pop$x,
  br = st_B[1:st_K], cr = st_C[1:st_K],
  estA = round(sapply(st_A, function(s) mean(s$y)), 4),
  estB = round(sapply(st_B, function(r) mean(pop$y[r == 1])), 4),
  estC = round(sapply(st_C, function(r) mean(pop$y[r == 1])), 4),
  estW = round(sapply(st_C, hajek), 4)
), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA)

# Stages (see the header of strip.js): 0-3 i.i.d. sampling, 4-7 a fixed finite
# population under SRS, 8-11 missingness that depends on X, 12-13 IPW
strip_anim <- function(from, to) {
  cat("```{=html}",
      '<div class="st-anim"></div>',
      "<script>",
      "(", readLines("strip-anim/strip.js"), ")(document.currentScript.previousElementSibling,",
      strip_data, ", { from: ", from, ", to: ", to, " });",
      "</script>",
      rep('<span class="fragment st-step"></span>', to - from),
      "```", sep = "\n")
}
```

<!-- ============================================================
     Where does the randomness come from?
     ============================================================ -->

## Where does uncertainty come from?

- We've spent a lot of time focusing on randomness from **sampling from a population**
     - Our **sample mean** is not the same as the **population mean**
     - Statistics gives us some tools for characterizing that error (**sampling variance**)

- But what happens if we have the **full population**?
     - All 193-197 countries in the world
     - All 50 states.
     - A set of *the specific villages* we're interested in.

- **Key idea**: Uncertainty comes from the stuff we **don't see**
     - And solutions require knowing the **mechanism** by which we don't see things!

## Sampling from a population {.strip-slide}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
strip_anim(0, 3)
```

## A finite population {.strip-slide}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
strip_anim(3, 7)
```

## Two sources of randomness

|                   | Sampling from $F$          | Finite population                       |
|-------------------|----------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| The values $Y_i$  | Random draws               | Fixed numbers                           |
| What's random     | Which values we draw       | Which units we see: $R_i$               |
| Estimand          | $\mu = \mathbb{E}[Y_i]$    | $\mu_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i$   |

::: {.incremental}

- Sampling from an **infinite population**: the cells stay, but the **values** change
- Finite population: the values stay, but the **holes** move

:::

<!-- ============================================================
     Finite population inference under simple random sampling
     ============================================================ -->

## A finite population

::: {.incremental}

- $N$ units with outcomes $Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_N$
  - These are **fixed numbers**, not random variables

- Estimand: the **population mean**

  $$\mu_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i$$

- and the **population variance**

  $$S^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N (Y_i - \mu_N)^2$$

- If we saw every $Y_i$, there's no uncertainty at all.

:::

## Simple random sampling

::: {.incremental}

- $R_i = 1$ if unit $i$ is in the sample, $R_i = 0$ if not, with $\sum_{i=1}^N R_i = n$

- **Simple random sampling** (SRS): each of the $\binom{N}{n}$ subsets of size $n$ is equally likely
     - Each unit has the same **inclusion probability**

     $$\Pr(R_i = 1) = \frac{n}{N}$$

- But the $R_i$ are **not independent**

  $$\Pr(R_i = 1, R_j = 1) = \frac{n}{N}\cdot\frac{n-1}{N-1} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Cov(R_i, R_j) = -\frac{1}{N-1}\cdot\frac{n}{N}\left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)$$

:::

## The sample mean is unbiased

::: {.incremental}

- We can write the sample mean as an average involving the inclusion indicator $R_i$

  $$\hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^N R_i Y_i$$

- The $Y_i$ are constants, so they come out of the expectation

  $$\mathbb{E}[\hat{\mu}] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}[R_i]\, Y_i = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{n}{N}\, Y_i = \mu_N$$

:::

## The variance of the sample mean

::: {.incremental}

- Recenter around the **mean** $\mu_N$

  $$\hat{\mu} - \mu_N = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^N R_i\,(Y_i - \mu_N)$$

- Only the $R_i$ are random

  $$\Var(\hat{\mu}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\Big[\sum_{i} (Y_i - \mu_N)^2\,\Var(R_i) + \sum_{i \neq j} (Y_i - \mu_N)(Y_j - \mu_N)\Cov(R_i, R_j)\Big]$$

- The covariance terms don't go away since the $R_i$ are **negatively** correlated

:::

## The variance of the sample mean

::: {.incremental}

- Deviations from the mean sum to zero, so

  $$\begin{aligned}
  0 = \Big(\sum_{i} (Y_i - \mu_N)\Big)^2 &= \sum_{i} (Y_i - \mu_N)^2 + \sum_{i \neq j} (Y_i - \mu_N)(Y_j - \mu_N) \\
  \Rightarrow \quad \sum_{i \neq j} (Y_i - \mu_N)(Y_j - \mu_N) &= -\sum_i (Y_i - \mu_N)^2
  \end{aligned}$$

- Plug in $\Var(R_i) = \frac{n}{N}\left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)$ and $\Cov(R_i, R_j) = -\frac{1}{N-1}\cdot\frac{n}{N}\left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)$

  $$\begin{aligned}
  \Var(\hat{\mu}) &= \frac{1}{n^2}\cdot\frac{n}{N}\left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\Big[\sum_i (Y_i - \mu_N)^2 + \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i (Y_i - \mu_N)^2\Big] \\
  &= \frac{1}{n^2}\cdot\frac{n}{N}\left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right) \cdot N \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i (Y_i - \mu_N)^2}_{S^2} \\
  &= \left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{S^2}{n}
  \end{aligned}$$

- $1 - \frac{n}{N}$ is the **finite population correction**: at $n = N$ (a census) the variance is $0$

:::

## Estimating the variance

::: {.incremental}

- Plug in the **sample** variance

  $$s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^N R_i\,(Y_i - \hat{\mu})^2 \qquad \widehat{\Var}(\hat{\mu}) = \left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{s^2}{n}$$

- Under SRS, $\mathbb{E}[s^2] = S^2$, so $\widehat{\Var}(\hat{\mu})$ is **exactly** unbiased

- A finite population CLT applies here [@hajek1960limiting]: as $n$ and $N - n$ grow

  $$\frac{\hat{\mu} - \mu_N}{\sqrt{\widehat{\Var}(\hat{\mu})}} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$$

- So the usual interval $\hat{\mu} \pm 1.96\sqrt{\widehat{\Var}(\hat{\mu})}$ works

:::

## From finite populations back to i.i.d.

::: {.incremental}

- As $N \to \infty$, $\frac{n}{N} \to 0$ and

  $$\Var(\hat{\mu}) = \left(1 - \frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{S^2}{n} \to \frac{\sigma^2}{n}$$

- Sampling without replacement from a huge population $\approx$ i.i.d. draws
  - The "infinite population" is a **limit** of the finite population seetting

- We can apply this idea beyond random sampling from a **finite population** to other forms of **missingness**

:::

## Simulating SRS in R

```{r}
#| label: srs-sim

# The animation's finite population: 24 fixed values; observe 10 of them
y <- pop$y; N <- length(y); n <- 10
set.seed(60706)
mu_hat <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(y, n)))   # sample() draws without replacement
c(mu_N = mean(y), mean_of_estimates = mean(mu_hat))
c(simulated = var(mu_hat), fpc_formula = (1 - n / N) * var(y) / n, iid_formula = var(y) / n)
```

<!-- ============================================================
     Missing data (Aronow and Miller 2019, Section 6.1)
     ============================================================ -->

## The missing data problem

::: {.incremental}

- For each unit we observe $(Y_i^*, R_i, X_i)$, where

  $$Y_i^* = \begin{cases} Y_i & R_i = 1 \\ \texttt{NA} & R_i = 0 \end{cases}$$

- $R_i$ works the same way (observability), but now it's **out of our control**
  - We don't know $\Pr(R_i = 1)$ and can't assume that $R_i$ is independent of $Y_i$

- Apply Law of Iterated/Total Expectation conditioning on $R_i$:

  $$\mathbb{E}[Y_i] = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid R_i = 1]\Pr(R_i = 1) + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid R_i = 0]}_{\text{never observed}}\Pr(R_i = 0)$$

:::

## Example: who won't report their income?

::: {.incremental}

- 2024 CES: "Thinking back over the last year, what was your family's annual income?"
  - `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(ces$R == 0))`% of `r format(nrow(ces), big.mark = ",")` respondents choose **"Prefer not to say"**

- $Y_i = 1$ if family income is **\$60,000 or more**, about the median among those who answer

- $X_i$: observed for everyone
  - Age, gender, education, race, employment, marital status, party ID, **political engagement**

- **Political engagement** - non-response to four questions on politics
  - Over the past year, has the nation's economy gotten better or worse?
  - Generally speaking, do you think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent...? (party ID)
  - In general, how would you describe your own political viewpoint? (ideology)
  - Do you follow what's going on in government and public affairs...? (interest)

:::


::: {.fragment .est-table}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ces |>
  mutate(unsure = if_else(unsure >= 3, "3 or 4", as.character(unsure))) |>
  group_by(unsure) |>
  summarize(n = format(n(), big.mark = ","),
            refused = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(R == 0)),
            above = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(inc60, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("\"Not sure\" answers", "Respondents", "Refuse income",
                             "Income $60k+ (if answered)"), align = "lrrr")
```

:::

## What can we learn without assumptions?

::: {.incremental}

- Suppose $Y_i \in [a, b]$. Then $\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid R_i = 0]$ is somewhere in $[a, b]$

- We can get **bounds** by plugging in the two extremes [@manski1989anatomy]

  $$\mathbb{E}[Y_i] \in \Big[\,\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid R_i = 1]\Pr(R_i = 1) + a\Pr(R_i = 0),\ \ \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid R_i = 1]\Pr(R_i = 1) + b\Pr(R_i = 0)\,\Big]$$


:::

## Bounds in the running example

```{r}
#| label: bounds

p_R <- mean(ces$R)
cc  <- mean(ces$inc60[ces$R == 1])                # the complete-case mean
c(complete_case = cc,
  lower = cc * p_R + 0 * (1 - p_R),               # every refuser earns under $60k
  upper = cc * p_R + 1 * (1 - p_R))               # every refuser earns $60k or more
```

::: {.incremental}

- `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(ces$R == 0))`% missing and a binary outcome: an interval `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(ces$R == 0))` percentage points wide
- To get a **point estimate** we need assumptions about $R_i$

:::

## Rubin's taxonomy

::: {.incremental}

- **Missing completely at random** (MCAR)

  $$R_i \indep Y_i$$

- **Missing at random** (MAR)

  $$R_i \indep Y_i \mid X_i$$

- **Missing not at random** (MNAR): neither holds

- Terms originated from @rubin1976inference - not the best language.
  - "At random" does **not** mean "random": MAR allows missingness to depend on $X_i$
  - Here "at random" is closer to "according to **known** non-randomness"

:::

## Missing completely at random

::: {.incremental}

- Under MCAR, respondents look like nonrespondents

  $$\mathbb{E}[Y_i] = \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid R_i = 1]$$

- The **complete-case** mean is consistent for $\mathbb{E}[Y_i]$
  - Missingness behaves like **random sampling** from a target population

:::

## Missing at random {.strip-slide}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
strip_anim(8, 11)
```

## Missing at random

::: {.incremental}

- MAR: **within** levels of $X_i$, missingness is unrelated to $Y_i$

  $$R_i \indep Y_i \mid X_i$$

- Plus **positivity**: Have to have some probability of responding at each covariate level.

  $$\Pr(R_i = 1 \mid X_i = x) > 0 \quad \text{for all } x$$

- MCAR within each **stratum** of $X_i$
     - But the response rate can **differ** across strata
     - The complete-case mean is **biased** when $X_i$ predicts both $R_i$ and $Y_i$

:::

## Identification under MAR

::: {.incremental}

- Law of iterated expectations, then MAR

  $$\mathbb{E}[Y_i] = \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i]\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid R_i = 1, X_i]\big]$$

  - Everything on the right is **observable**

- **Regression estimator**: fit $\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid R_i = 1, X_i]$ among respondents and predict for **everyone**

  $$\hat{\mu}_{\text{reg}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y_i \mid R_i = 1, X_i]$$

- Weighted average of outcomes among respondents
     - With weights **proportional** to $X_i$ distribution in the **full sample**

:::

## Missing not at random

::: {.incremental}

- Even given $X_i$, missingness depends on $Y_i$

  $$\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid R_i = 0, X_i] \neq \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid R_i = 1, X_i]$$

- Can't tell whether we're in MAR or MNAR from the data alone!
     - Analogous to **unobserved confounding** of response and outcome.

:::

<!-- ============================================================
     Inverse probability weighting (Aronow and Miller 2019, 6.1.4, 6.2.5)
     ============================================================ -->

## The propensity score for missingness

::: {.incremental}

- It turns out that we only need to know **one thing** in order to fully adjust for non-response bias. 
     - The **response propensity score**

     $$p_R(x) = \Pr(R_i = 1 \mid X_i = x)$$

- Under MAR, all we need to condition on is $p_R(X_i)$ [@rosenbaum1983central]

  $$R_i \indep Y_i \mid X_i \quad\Rightarrow\quad R_i \indep Y_i \mid p_R(X_i)$$

- Adjusting for the **propensity score** is as good as adjusting for all of $X_i$


:::

## Reweighting the respondents {.strip-slide}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
strip_anim(11, 13)
```

## Horvitz-Thompson

::: {.incremental}

- Our new estimator **re-weights** each respondent by the **inverse propensity** of response $1 / p_R(X_i)$ [@horvitz1952generalization]

  $$\hat{\mu}_{\text{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{R_i Y_i^*}{p_R(X_i)}$$

- This is the **Horvitz-Thompson** or **"inverse propensity weighting" (IPW)** estimator
- Can think of this as creating a **pseudo-population** where each respondent stands in for $1 / p_R(X_i)$ people like them.
     - **Under-represented** respondents count for more
     - **Over-represented** respondents count for less

:::

## Horvitz-Thompson is unbiased under MAR

::: {.incremental}

- With $p_R$ **known**, and since $R_i Y_i^* = R_i Y_i$

  $$\begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}[\hat{\mu}_{\text{HT}}] = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{R_i Y_i}{p_R(X_i)}\right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}[R_i Y_i \mid X_i]}{p_R(X_i)}\right] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}[R_i \mid X_i]\,\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i]}{p_R(X_i)}\right] \qquad \text{(MAR)} \\
  &= \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i]\big] = \mathbb{E}[Y_i]
  \end{aligned}$$

- Positivity ensures we don't divide by zero


:::

## Hájek

::: {.incremental}

- The HT weights $\frac{R_i}{p_R(X_i)}$ only sum to $n$ **on average**. 
     The **Hájek** estimator **(stabilized IPW)** normalizes them to sum to exactly 1 in the sample [@hajek1971comment]

  $$\hat{\mu}_{\text{Hájek}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{R_i Y_i^*}{p_R(X_i)}}{\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{R_i}{p_R(X_i)}}$$

- Has a clean interpretation as a **convex average** of the respondents
  - Slightly biased, consistent, usually **lower variance** than HT

:::

## IPW in the running example

```{r}
#| label: ipw

ps_fit <- glm(R ~ age + I(age^2) + educ + race + gender + employ + marstat + factor(pid7) +
                factor(pmin(unsure, 3)), family = binomial, data = ces)
ces <- ces |> mutate(p_hat = fitted(ps_fit), y_star = replace_na(inc60, 0))
ces |> summarize(complete_case = mean(inc60, na.rm = TRUE),
                 ht    = mean(R * y_star / p_hat),
                 hajek = sum(R * y_star / p_hat) / sum(R / p_hat))
```

::: {.incremental}

- Refusers are less engaged, and less engaged respondents earn less: weighting moves the estimate **down**, by `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * with(ces, mean(inc60, na.rm = TRUE) - sum(R * y_star / p_hat) / sum(R / p_hat)))` percentage points
- Weights run from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(1 / ces$p_hat[ces$R == 1]))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(1 / ces$p_hat[ces$R == 1]))`: the largest go to young students who are unsure about politics
- Why so small? Only `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(ces$R == 0))`% refuse. The shift is at most $\Pr(R_i = 0)$ times how different refusers look from respondents

:::

## Problems with weights

::: {.incremental}

- $\hat{p}_R(x)$ near $0$ means **huge** weights
  - A few respondents drive the estimate $\leadsto$ **massive variance**
  - Effective sample size: $n_{\text{eff}} = \big(\sum_i w_i\big)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2$

- **Positivity** fails: no respondents to re-weight to!

- **Misspecified** $\hat{p}_R$: the weights don't balance $X_i$
     - Solution: **balancing weights** - compute $\hat{p}_R$ such that we get exact balance on (functions of) $X_i$

- **Standard errors**: Need to account for uncertainty in estimating the weights.

:::
